mcqs.question: A team needs to ingest data from Salesforce, a widely-used SaaS tool with mature managed connectors available. What's the strongest reason to use a managed ingestion tool instead of hand-rolling the extraction?
options: A well-supported managed connector already handles pagination, rate limits, and schema drift, avoiding the upfront and ongoing engineering cost of solving the same problems again
Managed connectors are always cheaper than any engineering time spent building one
Hand-rolled extraction is technically impossible for SaaS APIs
Managed tools guarantee zero data loss while hand-rolled extraction cannot
mcqs.explanation: For a common, well-supported source, a managed connector has already solved the hard operational problems, so building your own mostly duplicates that work at ongoing engineering cost with no clear benefit. Hand-rolled extraction against SaaS APIs is entirely possible, cost comparisons depend on volume and pricing rather than being universally one-sided, and neither approach inherently guarantees zero data loss.

mcqs.question: Why is an orchestrator described as sitting apart from the data-flow layers rather than being just another stage data passes through?
options: Because orchestrators actually transform the data before passing it to the next stage
Because orchestrators only work with streaming pipelines, not batch ones
Because an orchestrator's job is deciding when and in what order other layers' jobs run, based on dependencies, rather than moving or transforming data itself
Because orchestrators replace the need for a warehouse or storage layer
mcqs.explanation: Orchestration is control-plane infrastructure about the other layers — sequencing and dependency management — rather than a stage where data itself is moved or changed, which is why it's drawn differently on the stack diagram. Orchestrators don't transform data, they work with both batch and streaming pipelines, and they have nothing to do with replacing storage.

mcqs.question: A small team with no dedicated infrastructure engineers is choosing between a fully managed warehouse and a self-managed lakehouse on S3. Which factor most strongly favors the managed option?
options: Managed warehouses are always less expensive at every possible scale
Self-managed lakehouses cannot separate storage from compute
Managed warehouses provide better SQL syntax than any self-managed alternative
The team avoids the ongoing operational burden of running and tuning the underlying infrastructure themselves
mcqs.explanation: The core buy-vs-build trade-off is operational ownership versus cost and control — a team without dedicated infra engineers benefits most from offloading that ongoing operational burden to a managed vendor. Cost comparisons vary heavily by scale and usage pattern rather than favoring one option universally, storage/compute separation is exactly what a lakehouse does provide, and SQL syntax quality isn't the deciding factor here.

mcqs.question: A team adopts Spark for a dataset that comfortably fits in memory on a single machine, reasoning they'll need it "for the future." What's the likely practical outcome?
options: The job runs identically fast regardless of cluster overhead
The Spark job may run slower than a single-node alternative due to coordination and data-shuffling overhead, while costing more to operate
Spark cannot process small datasets at all and the job will fail outright
Adopting Spark early guarantees a smoother migration whenever the dataset does grow
mcqs.explanation: Spark's distributed coordination and data-shuffling costs are real overhead that a small, memory-fitting dataset doesn't need to pay, so the simpler single-node approach can actually be faster and cheaper in that regime. Spark will run, just inefficiently; it won't fail outright, and adopting it early doesn't meaningfully guarantee an easier future migration compared to adopting it once the actual scale need appears.
